BLASTr: Parallel Taxonomic Classification of Metabarcoding Sequences

Overview

BLASTr is an R package that seamlessly integrates BLAST+ searches into your R workflow. It is specifically designed for the analysis of amplicon sequences from metabarcoding and metagenomic studies. With BLASTr, you can efficiently perform taxonomic classification of your sequences by leveraging the power of parallel processing and automated dependency management.

Features

  • Parallel BLAST Searches: Sequences are searched in batches, with the number of processes and threads chosen from your cores, RAM and database size. Searches can run in the background, with progress and ETA.
  • Automated Dependency Management: BLASTr automatically installs and manages BLAST+ and Entrez Direct dependencies using condathis, ensuring a hassle-free setup.
  • Taxonomic Classification: Retrieve detailed taxonomic information for your sequences using their NCBI Taxonomy IDs.
  • Flexible and Easy to Use: The package provides a set of intuitive functions that simplify the process of running thousands of BLAST searches and handling the results.
  • Reproducible Research: By managing dependencies in isolated Conda environments, BLASTr helps ensure that your analyses are reproducible.

Installation

You can install the development version of BLASTr from GitHub with:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("heronoh/BLASTr")

Basic Usage

Here’s a simple example of how to use BLASTr to perform a BLAST search and retrieve taxonomic information:

Obtain NCBI databases

To obtain complet NCBI blast formated databases, procees as follows

#suggestion: use screen or tmux to emulate a terminal. The downloads usually takes long.
#          tmux: https://tmuxcheatsheet.com/
#          screen: https://kapeli.com/cheat_sheets/screen.docset/Contents/Resources/Documents/index

# download volumes and md5 check files 
seq -w 000 150 | parallel wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast/db/nt.{}.tar.gz -t 0 --show-progress;
seq -w 000 150 | parallel wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast/db/nt.{}.tar.gz.md5 -t 0 --show-progress;
wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast/db/taxdb.tar.gz -t 0 --show-progress;
wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast/db/taxdb.tar.gz.md5 -t 0 --show-progress;
wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast/db/taxdb-metadata.json -t 0 --show-progress;
     # where 000 is the first volume and 150, the last (up to now).
     
ls *5 | parallel md5sum -c {} >> check.txt
sort check.txt > check_sort.txt

ls *tar.gz | parallel tar -xvzf {} 

Making local custom databeses

You can turn any .fasta file with unique headers into a BLAST+ formated database using the BLASTr function make_blast_db. It is recomended that the unique identifier of each sequence do not contain .. You may provide a .txt with the same name as the DB’s .fasta file, formated lcl|.

If you want to retrieve subject Scientific name on the results, you can download and extract the taxdb files from NCBI, as mentioned above.

library(BLASTr)

# First, make sure you have the necessary dependencies installed
install_dependencies()

# A vector of query sequences
seqs <- c(
  "CTAGCCATAAACTTAAATGAAGCTATACTAAACTCGTTCGCCAGAGTACTACAAGCGAAAGCTTAAAACTCATAGGACTTGGCGGTGTTTCAGACCCAC",
  "CTAGCCATAAACTTAAATGAAGCTATACTAAACTCGTTCGCCAGAGTACTACAAGTGAAAGCTTAAAACTCATAGGACTTGGCGGTGTTTCAGACCCAC",
  "GCCAAATTTGTGTTTTGTCCTTCGTTTTTAGTTAATTGTTACTGGCAAATGACTAACGACAAATGATAAATTACTAATAC",
  "AACATTGTATTTTGTCTTTGGGGCCTGGGCAGGTGCAGTAGGAACTTCACTTAGAATAATTATTCGTACTGAGCTTGGGCATCCAGGAAGACTTATCGGGGATGATCAAATCTATAATGTAATTGTTACAGCACATGCATTTGTGATAATTTTTTTTATAGTAATACCTATTATGATT",
  "ACTATACCTATTATTCGGCGCATGAGCTGGAGTCCTAGGCACAGCTCTAAGCCTCCTTATTCGAGCCGAGCTGGGCCAGCCAGGCAACCTTCTAGGTAACGACCACATCTACAACGTTATCGTCACAGCCCATGCATTTGTAATAATCTTCTTCATAGTAATACCCATCATAATCGGAGGCTTTGGCAACTGACTAGTTCCCCTAATAATCGGTGCCCCCGATATG",
  "TTAGCCATAAACATAAAAGTTCACATAACAAGAACTTTTGCCCGAGAACTACTAGCAACAGCTTAAAACTCAAAGGACTTGGCGGTGCTTTATATCCAC"
)

# Path to your local FASTA database
fasta_path <- fs::path_package("BLASTr", "extdata", "minimal_db_blast", ext = "fasta")
# Path to database
db_path <- fs::path_temp("minimal_db_blast")

# To add taxids, pass `taxid_map`: a .txt file with the same name and
#  directory as the FASTA, with two columns separated by a space. The 1st is
#  the unique ID (first word of the header, no "."), preceded by "lcl|";
#  the 2nd is the taxID.

make_blast_db(
  fasta_path = fasta_path,
  db_path = db_path,
  db_type = "nucl"
)

head(readLines(fasta_path))

file.exists(paste0(db_path, ".ndb"))

# For `ssciname` (subject scientific name) to work, BLAST must find the
#  taxdb files: export BLASTDB pointing to their directory, e.g.
#  export BLASTDB=/data/databases/core_nt:$BLASTDB
# Run BLAST in parallel
blast_results <- parallel_blast(
  query_seqs = seqs,
  db_path = db_path,
  total_cores = 2 # Total number of threads to use
)

blast_results

How the search is split

parallel_blast() groups the sequences in batches and runs one blastn per batch, so the database is read once per batch instead of once per sequence. How many blastn run at once, with how many threads each, and how many sequences go in each batch are chosen automatically from total_cores, ram_gb (the RAM available for the search; the total RAM of the machine by default), the size of the database(s) and the number of sequences. blast_strategy() shows the plan without running BLAST:

blast_strategy(
  n_seqs = 2000,
  db_path = "/data/databases/core_nt/core_nt",
  total_cores = 32,
  ram_gb = 256
)

num_threads, batch_size and mt_mode override the automatic choice. Several databases can be given as a vector in db_path; they are searched together, smallest first.

While BLAST runs, a progress bar shows the percentage done and the estimated time left (ETA).

Running in the background

With background = TRUE, parallel_blast() starts the search in a separate process and returns a job at once, so the R session (or a pipeline run in blocks) is free in the meantime. The job lives in a directory and survives the end of the R session.

job <- parallel_blast(
  query_seqs = seqs,
  db_path = db_path,
  total_cores = 2,
  background = TRUE
)

blast_job_status(job) # progress and ETA
blast_results <- blast_job_result(job) # waits for the end if needed

# From another R session:
# job <- blast_job("<job directory>")
# blast_job_cancel(job); blast_job_resume(job)

Results

By default (output = "long") each row is a hit, best first. The hits of each sequence are ranked by BLASTr, not by BLAST’s order (which favours long alignments): by the Similarity score ((10 * identity + qcovhsp) / 11; or rank_by = "identity" / "bitscore"), then identity, coverage and bitscore. The Similarity score weighs identity ten times more than coverage: a reference that covers less of the sequence is penalised only a little, since a part not covered is missing information, not a difference. In a calibration with sequences of known taxonomy (87 plant barcodes, ITS2 and rbcL, of genus confirmed by two markers; 1257 GenBank references of six markers searched without themselves), the first hit by Similarity score or by identity had the right genus or species significantly more often than the first hit by bitscore (plant barcodes: right genus in 72% and 76% against 62%; GenBank, species: 9 and 15 cases right only with them against 1 and 3 only with bitscore), with no significant difference between Similarity score and identity.

BLAST searches with a low coverage cutoff (search_qcov_hsp = 50): a closer reference that covers a bit less of the query is kept, not replaced by a worse one. Hits below perc_qcov_hsp = 80 are flagged (low_qcov), and the coverage weighs in the Similarity score.

References that say little about the query are set aside when ranking (uninformative, the table of uninformative_references()): uncultured or unidentified organisms, metagenomes and MAGs, environmental samples, synthetic constructs and vectors, chimeras, and specific references known to be wrong. Their taxid is often only “Bacteria” or “environmental samples”, so they should not decide the identification when a named organism is also among the hits. The hits are flagged (informative, uninformative_category) and ranked among the informative ones; a sequence whose hits are all uninformative keeps its best ones, ranked among themselves. The table is versioned in the package (its md5 is in the metadata); uninformative = NULL treats all hits alike.

  • rank: 1 is the best hit; tied hits share the rank (tie = TRUE). Uninformative hits, when there are informative ones, come last with rank NA.
  • at_best: the hit is within check_tolerance = 0.5 of the best one, a tied candidate for the identification. All hits at best are kept, even beyond num_alignments (10 by default).
  • blast_rank: the order given by BLAST.
  • The hit fields: subject, subject header, staxid, identity, Similarity score, qcovhsp, nident, length, mismatches, gaps, query start, query end, subject start, subject end, subject strand, e-value and bitscore.

A sequence without hits has one row with empty hit fields. blast_summary() gives one row per sequence:

  • Check ID: "best ID" when the best hits (the first check_n = 10) at best agree on the taxid, "check ID" when they do not. Hits with unknown taxid (0) never confirm an identification.
  • N hits, N taxids, N hits same taxid as 1st, N hits at best and N taxids at best. N hits at best = 1 means the "best ID" rests on a single reference; several hits with one taxid at best mean several references agreeing.
  • Taxids at best: the taxids tied with the best hit, for a lowest common ancestor; At best truncated: the tie may go beyond the subjects BLAST returned (search_alignments).
  • Best low qcov: the best hit covers less than perc_qcov_hsp of the query.
  • N uninformative and Best uninformative score: uninformative hits among the first num_alignments, and the best value of rank_by among them. Above the best informative hit, the sequence is closer to an uncultured or environmental sequence than to any named organism: a sign of a taxon missing from the database.
summary <- blast_summary(blast_results)
best <- blast_results[blast_results$rank %in% 1L, ]

output = "wide" gives one row per sequence: Sequence, the summary and the hits side by side (1_subject, 1_identity, …) in rank order. as_blast_long() converts wide results, of this or older versions, to the long format.

The BLAST command (without the sequences), the BLAST version and the date of each database are kept in attr(blast_results, "BLASTr_metadata") (blast_cmd, blast_version, db_dates); the command is shown in interactive sessions.

BLASTr keeps track of any errors that may occur during the BLAST searches. You can retrieve the exit codes and STDERR messages using the exit_codes() function.

# Check for any errors during BLAST searches
exit_code_df <- exit_codes(blast_results)
print(exit_code_df[c("exit_code", "stderr")])

Taxonomy

get_tax() reads the NCBI taxonomy from a local SQLite database. It takes taxids or a BLASTr result and returns one row per taxid, with the ranks, the full lineage and its lineage_taxids. blast_lca() gives, for each sequence, the deepest taxon that holds at least 90% of the hits tied with the best one (consensus): one mislabelled reference among many tied hits does not push the identification up to a high rank, and with up to 9 tied hits all of them must agree. Hits named only above genus (“Bacterium”, “Entolomataceae sp.”) do not vote when a named species is tied with them (named_first), while “Picea sp.” still does (another species of the genus). When that taxon has no standard rank (e.g. the clade “Heliantheae alliance”), LCA name keeps it and LCA ranked name / LCA ranked rank give the nearest ranked taxon above it (here the subfamily Asteroideae). If the database does not exist, it is built once from the NCBI taxdump: for a BLASTr result, the taxdump published right after the date of its BLAST database, so the taxonomy matches the database (about a minute, then kept in the BLASTr cache).

taxonomy <- get_tax(blast_results)

# taxon shared by the hits tied with the best one (90% consensus)
lca <- blast_lca(blast_results)

# or a database of your choice, built from a given taxdump if missing
taxonomy <- get_tax(c("9606", "10090"), taxonomy_db = "~/databases/taxonomy.sqlite")
dplyr::left_join(blast_results, taxonomy, by = c(staxid = "taxid"))

Performance

In the development version, parallel_blast() groups the sequences in batches instead of running one blastn per sequence. Each blastn reads the whole database once per batch, so on large databases the gain is large. Benchmark on a shared server (80 threads, 503 GB RAM, rotational disks) with BLAST+ 2.16.0 and NCBI core_nt (299 GB in 92 volumes, all in RAM unless stated), searching sets of amplicon sequences:

Search Sequences Before (one blastn per sequence, 32 at a time) Now (automatic strategy)
core_nt in RAM 100 944 s 79 s
core_nt read from disk 100 1296 s 441 s
core_nt in RAM 500 6138 s (1 run) 168 s

CPU time fell in the same proportion: 0.26 CPU-hours against 6.9 for the same 100 sequences searched one per blastn. In the tests with 100 sequences the first hit was the same for every sequence, and so were the sequences with and without hits; with 500 sequences, the batched search found a hit for one sequence more (293 against 292).

What drives the automatic strategy (see blast_strategy()):

  • Threads per blastn: with 32 threads blastn splits the database among them (-mt_mode 2). More threads in one process did not help: with 500 / 2000 sequences, 1 blastn with 64 threads took 152 s / 265 s against 120 s / 206 s with 32. Extra cores go to more processes: 2 processes of 32 threads took 87 s / 182 s.
  • Fewer, larger batches: each batch reads the database again (about 70 s on core_nt). With 4 processes of 8 threads, 2000 sequences in 80 batches took 1194 s; in 4 batches, 345 s.
  • Database larger than the RAM: each batch reads it from disk, so all sequences go in one batch.
  • Number of hits: keeping 1 to 50 hits per sequence took 71 s to 91 s for 100 sequences, so the default is 10 hits, searched among 50.

The benchmark scripts are in dev/benchmark/. Times depend on the machine and on the load of a shared server; they are a guide, not a guarantee. log_dir keeps a log of your own searches (see blast_log_path()).

Main Functions

  • install_dependencies(): Installs BLAST+ and Entrez Direct if they are not found on your system.
  • make_blast_db(): Creates a BLAST database from a FASTA file.
  • parallel_blast(): Runs BLAST searches for multiple sequences in parallel, in the foreground or in the background.
  • parallel_blast_hsps(): Like parallel_blast(), but returns every HSP in long format, against a database or a FASTA file (subject).
  • blast_log_path(), read_blast_log(): Optional log of the searches (log_dir).
  • blast_strategy(): Shows how parallel_blast() will split a search.
  • blast_job_status(), blast_job_result(), blast_job_cancel(), blast_job_resume(): Follow a search running in the background.
  • blast_summary(), check_hits(), similarity_score(): Summary per sequence (Check ID, ties) and Similarity score.
  • as_blast_long(): Converts wide results (any version) to the long format.
  • exit_codes(): Retrieve the exit codes and STDERR messages from BLAST searches.
  • get_tax(), make_taxonomy_db(): Taxonomy of NCBI taxids from a local database.
  • blast_lca(): Consensus lowest common ancestor of the best hits.
  • uninformative_references(): The references set aside when ranking the hits.
  • run_blast(): A lower-level function to run a BLAST search and return the raw output.
  • parse_fasta(): Extracts sequences from a FASTA file.
  • get_fasta_header(): Retrieves the full header of a sequence from a BLAST database.

Dependency Management

BLASTr uses the condathis package to manage its dependencies (BLAST+ and Entrez Direct). When you run a function that requires one of these tools, BLASTr will automatically check if it’s installed. If not, it will create a Conda environment and install the necessary software. This ensures that you always have the correct versions of the dependencies without having to install them manually.

You can control the installation process with the force and verbose arguments in the install_dependencies() function.
